metadata.purpose: Provide background on China-related national security concerns in US data center policy
metadata.note: This section should be included in dashboard documentation or as a linked reference, but is NOT a moratorium entry. It provides context for understanding the federal national security framework that constrains Chinese participation in US data center development.

section.title: China-Related National Security Concerns: Federal Framework (Reference)
section.scope: Preventing Chinese ownership, control, or strategic access to US data center infrastructure and AI compute capacity
section.summary_for_dashboard: China-related national security concerns are addressed primarily through federal mechanisms (CFIUS committee review, export controls on AI chips, intelligence community counterintelligence) rather than state-level moratoriums. Congressional leadership from both parties views Chinese investment in US data center infrastructure and access to AI compute as national security threats equivalent to weapons proliferation. Federal barriers are sufficient to prevent Chinese participation; state moratoriums focus on environmental concerns (energy, water, planning) while operating within this federal security framework.

key_federal_mechanisms.mechanism: CFIUS (Committee on Foreign Investment in US)
key_federal_mechanisms.action: Mandatory national security review and potential blocking of Chinese acquisitions in data center and critical tech sectors
key_federal_mechanisms.example: ByteDance prohibited from owning US data center infrastructure

key_federal_mechanisms.action: Bans specified Chinese firms from US trade and data center equipment supply
examples: Huawei: Comprehensive ban from US data center equipment (2019-2024)
ZTE: Restricted from US government and critical infrastructure contracts

key_federal_mechanisms.action: Restrict NVIDIA H100/H200, AMD MI300 exports to China
key_federal_mechanisms.objective: Prevent China from acquiring AI compute capacity equivalent to US data centers

key_federal_mechanisms.action: Active operations against Chinese espionage targeting US data centers and AI chip manufacturers

congressional_consensus.statement: Bipartisan consensus: Chinese entities must not control or operate US data center infrastructure
key_voices: Tom Cotton (R-AR) — Senate Armed Services Committee
Marco Rubio (R-FL) — Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chair
congressional_consensus.framing: Treated as national security threat equivalent to weapons proliferation

state_moratorium_relationship.finding: State-level data center moratoriums do NOT explicitly cite China concerns
state_moratorium_relationship.primary_drivers: Environmental (energy grid, water scarcity) and planning concerns
state_moratorium_relationship.delegation: States delegate national security vetting to federal authorities
state_moratorium_relationship.current_record: No state-level moratoriums explicitly name China or Chinese companies
state_moratorium_relationship.implication: Federal barriers are sufficient to prevent Chinese participation; states focus on local environmental impacts

chinese_investment_status.direct_ownership: Limited current direct ownership; de facto prohibited through CFIUS review

companies_restricted.name: ByteDance
companies_restricted.status: Prohibited from US data center ownership

documented_operations.name: APT41
documented_operations.targets: US tech companies, cloud providers, data center operators
documented_operations.objective: IP theft, AI chip designs, proprietary technology

ai_chips.restriction: Strict export controls to China; requires Commerce Dept license (generally denied)
ai_chips.objective: Prevent China from acquiring AI compute capacity equivalent to US

export_controls_status.strategic_objective: Maintain US AI technological dominance; prevent China from catching up
export_controls_status.chinese_workaround: Developing domestic alternatives (Huawei Kunpeng, Alibaba Yitian) but trailing by 2-3 years
export_controls_status.allied_coordination: Japan, South Korea, Netherlands aligning on semiconductor equipment restrictions

why_states_dont_cite_china: Environmental impacts (energy, water) are immediate local concerns; national security is federal domain
CFIUS review and export controls already prevent Chinese participation
State legislators delegate national security vetting to federal authorities
Explicit China language would be politically sensitive; environmental framing is safer
Federal barriers are sufficient; states don't need to duplicate restrictions
section.future_trajectory: If Congress passes explicit legislation tightening foreign investment rules in data centers, state moratoriums may evolve to include explicit national security language. However, current preference is federal-level enforcement through CFIUS and commerce controls.
